_doc: The dictionary's own table of English inflections that the rules in tools/inflect.py cannot predict, written from the project's knowledge; nothing here is copied from an external data set. American forms are primary; a note records the British or alternative form. Sections: verbs {base: {past_tense, past_participle, third_person_singular?, present_participle?, note?}} (a missing third person or participle is made by the rules); nouns {singular: plural string | null (no plural) | [alternatives, first shown] | {plural, also?, note?}}; adjectives and adverbs {base: {comparative, superlative, note?}} (null forms with a note mean the word is not gradable or compares with more); doubling (words of more than one syllable whose final consonant doubles before -ed, -ing, -er, -est); single_l (American single l where British doubles: traveled, travelled); keep_e (the final e stays before -ing); ie_to_y (-ie becomes -ying); o_es (nouns and verbs that take -es after o); f_to_ves (-f or -fe becomes -ves); c_ck (a k is added before -ed and -ing); suffix_regular (words ending in -man that take -s). A word is looked up in lower case; a hyphenated or spaced headword is looked up whole, then by its last word. Add a line here, in the same pull request as the entry that needs it, when a form is unpredictable.

bear.note: born in the passive of giving birth

beat.note: also beat as past participle, informal

bid.note: bade and bidden in the old meaning of ordering or greeting

cost.note: costed when the meaning is to estimate the cost of something

dive.note: also dived as the past tense

fit.note: also fitted, especially British and for the meaning of installing something

get.note: also got as the past participle, as in have got; British English uses got

lie.note: lie meaning tell an untruth is regular: lied

plead.note: also pled, especially in American legal use

read.note: the past forms are spelled read but pronounced like red

shine.note: shined when the meaning is to polish

shrink.note: also shrunk as the past tense; shrunken as a past participle before a noun

slay.note: slayed in the informal meaning of impressing an audience

speed.note: speeded when the meaning is to speed something up

spit.note: also spit as past tense and past participle in American English

stride.note: also strode as the past participle

weave.note: weaved when the meaning is to move in and out

wind.note: wind meaning to make someone short of breath is regular: winded

shave.note: shaven before a noun: a clean-shaven face

antenna.note: antennae for the feelers of insects and in scientific use; antennas for radio and television

die.note: dies for the tool that shapes metal

fish.note: fishes for different kinds of fish

medium.note: media for means of communication and for materials; mediums for people who claim to speak with the dead

mouse.note: also mouses for the computer device

octopus.note: octopi is common but disputed; octopodes is rare

penny.note: pence for an amount of money in British English; pennies for the coins

person.note: persons in formal and legal use

pike.note: pike for the fish; pikes for the weapon

staff.note: also staves for the set of lines that music is written on

brother.note: brethren for members of a religious group or a fellowship

fun.note: comparative with more; funner and funnest are informal

late.note: latter and last in some meanings

little.note: littler and littlest for size, informal

near.note: next in the meaning of the one coming after

old.note: elder and eldest for members of a family

often.note: comparative with more; oftener is rare
